theme: You will not abandon my soul to Sheol
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 16. David’s confidence in the LORD reaches past death. Both Peter in Acts 2 and Paul in Acts 13 quote verse 10 as a prophecy of the resurrection of Jesus.
settingTheScene: Psalm 16 is a “miktam” of David, a poem of trust. David asks for protection and then declares that the LORD is his chosen portion. The mood is quiet and joyful confidence. The psalm ends with a hope that goes beyond what David himself experienced, which is why Peter says David “foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ.”
observation: “Preserve me, O God, for in you I take refuge” (v. 1).
“I say to the LORD, You are my Lord; I have no good apart from you” (v. 2).
“The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot” (v. 5).
“The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance” (v. 6).
“I bless the LORD who gives me counsel; in the night also my heart instructs me” (v. 7).
“I have set the LORD always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken” (v. 8).
“For you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption” (v. 10).
“You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (v. 11).
interpretation:
David begins by taking refuge: “Preserve me, O God, for in you I take refuge.” He affirms that the LORD is his Lord and that he has no good apart from him. All his delight is in the saints in the land, the people of God. Those who run after other gods multiply their sorrows.

Then the heart of the psalm: “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot.” In Israel, each tribe received a portion of land, except Levi, whose portion was the LORD himself. David applies this to himself. The LORD is his inheritance. The boundary lines have fallen in pleasant places. Having God, he has everything.

He blesses the LORD for counsel, even at night, and sets the LORD always before him. Because God is at his right hand, he will not be shaken. “Therefore my heart is glad, and my whole being rejoices; my flesh also dwells secure.”

Then comes verse 10: “For you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption.” In David’s own situation, this is a confident hope of rescue from death. But Peter says on Pentecost that David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. David was a prophet and knew God had sworn to set one of his descendants on his throne. “He foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption.” The ultimate holy one is Jesus, whom God raised up. Paul argues in Acts 13:35-37 the same way.

The psalm ends with the path of life: “in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore.” This is the believer’s hope too. Because Christ rose, we too will be raised. The presence of God is not just a duty but a joy that never ends.
connection: Numbers 18:20 and Deuteronomy 10:9 say the LORD is the Levites’ inheritance. Psalm 73:25-26 also says God is my portion. Psalm 17:15 expresses the hope of beholding God. Acts 2:25-32 and 13:35-37 quote and explain verse 10. 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 says Christ is the firstfruits of the resurrection. Hebrews 12:2 says Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before him. Matthew 5:8 promises that the pure in heart will see God.
application:
Say “You are my Lord; I have no good apart from you” as a prayer. What other goods compete for your heart?

Thank God for the beautiful inheritance of being his child.

Meditate on verse 11. What would it mean to live today in the path of life?
prayerPrompts: Tell God that you have no good apart from him.
Thank him for the beautiful inheritance he has given you.
Thank him that he will not abandon your soul.
